title: Managing Up: Talking to Non-Technical Leaders
summary: When a leader asks "are we almost done?", give an answer they can decide on: the conclusion first, impact before mechanism, real options and a number for confidence.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Thursday afternoon, the release review is almost over when the head of sales leans back and asks, "So, are we almost done?" The honest answer has five parts. The API is stable. The migration passed on staging. One payment integration still fails now and then. The rollback plan is decent, though not perfect. And the partner's sandbox has been down since Tuesday. All true, and none of it fits the question.

You can answer that with a shrug, a wall of jargon or a nervous "yeah, mostly." Or you can answer it in a way that helps the person decide something. This post is about the last option.

What managing up actually is

Managing up sounds like office politics. In practice it's simpler: helping the people above and around your team make good decisions with the technical reality in front of them. You aren't there to please them, hide bad news or sell anything.

It helps to remember what those leaders carry. A head of sales has promised a date to a customer. Finance has a forecast that assumes the launch. Legal may have a contract clause attached to it. When they ask "are we done?", they aren't doubting your skills. They're trying to figure out which of their own promises are still safe.

Will Larson, who has led engineering at several tech companies, notes that conversations with executives are "almost always one of three things: planning, reporting on status, or resolving misalignment" (Present to executives). Knowing which of the three you're in tells you what to bring. Planning needs options. Status needs a clear read on risk. Misalignment needs a proposal people can agree or disagree with.

Put the answer first

Engineers like to build up to the conclusion, because that's how we got there: context, then investigation, then findings. Leaders hear the first two minutes as noise and spend them wondering whether the news is good or bad.

Larson borrows a rule from Barbara Minto's pyramid principle: "The clearest sequence is always to give the summarizing idea before you give the individual ideas being summarized." For the Thursday question, that sounds like this:

Answer first, details second

"Short answer: not at full scope by Friday. We can ship Friday to 10% of users, or ship to everyone next Wednesday. I'd go with the 10% rollout. Here's why, and what each option costs."

Now the details have a frame. When you mention the flaky integration, everyone knows why it matters.

Impact first, then the mechanism

A common slip is reporting artifacts instead of consequences. "The event schema changed." "The SDK upgrade has a breaking change." "The cache layer isn't ready." Those facts matter, but without the meaning attached, a non-technical listener hears weather.

Flip the order. "The main risk is that invoices could go out late for a small group of customers. The reason: our billing provider changed how one webhook behaves, and our retry logic doesn't handle the new behavior safely yet." The first sentence is the business picture. The second gives just enough mechanism to show the risk is real.

Keeping it simple doesn't mean flattening the problem. Nobody needs every SQL statement in a risky migration, but leaders do need its shape: how many customers it could touch, how sure you are, how you'd roll back, how long the risky window lasts, and whether support should prepare a message.

Bring options to the meeting

"We're blocked" gives a leader nothing to do except worry. A short set of options gives them a decision. Leaders can work with options. Fog is what makes them anxious, and anxious leaders tend to fill the gap with deadlines.

Option What you get What it costs Our confidence
A. Ship Friday to 10% of users Real traffic on the new flow this week Most customers wait until the next week High. We can turn it off in minutes.
B. Ship to everyone on Wednesday One launch, full scope Five more days. Marketing moves the email. About 80%. Depends on the partner fixing their sandbox.
C. Ship Friday to everyone, without saved cards The date holds Repeat buyers type their card again High, but support expects more tickets.

Three options are usually plenty. Say which one you'd pick and why. Then accept that the leader may pick another one for reasons you can't see from where you sit, like a promise made to a big customer last month.

Separate facts from judgment, and put a number on it

Facts are what the team knows: the error rate, the missing approval, the failing test, the partner's sandbox status. Judgment is what you think those facts mean: the risk sits in one flow, and the safest path is a gradual rollout. Mix the two and people either over-trust your conclusion or end up arguing with your mood.

Judgment words are slippery, and that has been documented for a long time. In 1951, U.S. intelligence analysts called a Soviet-bloc attack on Yugoslavia "a serious possibility." When Sherman Kent asked his colleagues on the Board of National Estimates what odds they had meant, the answers ranged from about 20 to 80 up to 80 to 20, for the same phrase they had all signed off on (Words of Estimative Probability).

Your "probably Friday" has the same problem. Say "about 70% for Friday, and the big unknown is the partner's sandbox" instead. If the number feels too precise, give a range. Either way, the leader can now plan around it.

Say it early, and ask what matters most

Bad news gets harder to take once everyone has repeated the old plan in other rooms. If your confidence drops from 90% to 60%, say so while there's still time to change course. An early heads-up with a number is much easier to work with than a dramatic escalation two days before launch.

Managing up also means asking questions back. What matters most for this release: the date, the full scope, reliability, or cost? Would it hurt more to launch late or to launch with one known limitation? Who needs to hear before the plan changes? The answers often make the technical decision obvious. For the written side of this, see writing status updates people can act on.

Try this week

  • Rewrite your next status update so the first sentence is the answer.
  • Replace one "probably" with a percentage and the single biggest unknown behind it.
  • Next time you're blocked, bring two or three options with costs instead of the word "blocked."
  • Ask your manager or stakeholder which matters most this quarter: date, scope or reliability. Write the answer down.

faqs.q: What does managing up mean for an engineer?
faqs.a: Helping the people above and around your team make good decisions with the technical reality in front of them. That means giving clear answers, real options and honest confidence levels. It has nothing to do with pleasing leaders or hiding bad news.

faqs.q: How do I explain a technical risk to a non-technical leader?
faqs.a: Start with the business impact, then give just enough mechanism to show the risk is real. For example, say invoices may go out late for some customers, then explain that a provider changed a webhook and your retry logic doesn't handle it yet. Add how many customers it could touch, how you would roll back and how sure you are.

faqs.q: Why should I give a percentage instead of saying 'probably'?
faqs.a: People read the same word very differently. In 1951, members of a U.S. intelligence board who had all approved the phrase 'serious possibility' meant odds ranging from roughly 20 to 80 up to 80 to 20, as Sherman Kent later described. A number with its main unknown leaves much less room for misreading.

faqs.q: What should I do instead of saying 'we're blocked'?
faqs.a: Bring two or three options, each with what you get, what it costs and how confident you are. Say which one you recommend and why, then let the leader choose. They may know about commitments that change the answer.

faqs.q: When should I tell leadership that a date is at risk?
faqs.a: As soon as your confidence drops in a way that could change their plans, while there is still time to act. An early warning with a number and a reason is much easier to handle than a late escalation after the old date has been repeated to customers.
